profile.summary: VESPA predicts the effect of single amino acid substitutions in a protein from the sequence alone, with no multiple sequence alignment and no structure. It embeds the sequence with the ProtT5 protein language model, predicts how conserved each residue is, extracts the language model's log-odds ratios for each substitution, and feeds all of that together with BLOSUM62 substitution scores into a logistic regression ensemble that outputs an effect score for every possible substitution. The authors report it as competitive with alignment-based predictors on deep mutational scanning data, although it was fitted without any such data.

summary_quotes.text: **VESPA** is a simple, yet powerful Single Amino Acid Variant (SAV) effect predictor based on embeddings of the Protein Language Model

Inputting the conservation prediction along with BLOSUM62 substitution scores and pLM mask reconstruction probabilities into a simplistic logistic regression (LR) ensemble for Variant Effect Score Prediction without Alignments (VESPA) predicted SAV effect magnitude without any optimization on DMS data.
revealed our approach as competitive with the state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods using MSA input

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: VESPA runs a pipeline of four steps. First it embeds the sequence with ProtT5. Second it predicts per-residue conservation in nine classes from that embedding, as defined by ConSurf-DB. Third it extracts per-variant log-odds ratios of masked marginal probabilities from ProtT5. Fourth it feeds the conservation prediction, BLOSUM62 substitution scores and those mask reconstruction probabilities into a balanced logistic regression ensemble, which outputs the effect score. The ensemble is ten logistic regressions trained on rotated cross-validation splits of Eff10k, a set of 100,737 binary variant effect annotations from 9,594 proteins, sharing one set of hyper-parameters. No deep mutational scanning data was used to fit it.

quotes.text: The single-sequence-based SAV effect prediction is set up in a multistage pipeline that includes (1) generating `ProtT5` embeddings, (2) extracting per-residue conservation predictions, (3) (optionally) extracting per-variant log-odds ratios, and (4) predicting the effect of all possible amino acid substitutions.

Inputting the conservation prediction along with BLOSUM62 substitution scores and pLM mask reconstruction probabilities into a simplistic logistic regression (LR) ensemble for Variant Effect Score Prediction without Alignments (VESPA) predicted SAV effect magnitude without any optimization on DMS data.
we trained a balanced logistic regression (LR) ensemble method as implemented in SciKit
We rotated the ten splits of Eff10k, such that each data split was used exactly once for testing, while all remaining splits were used for training.
It contained 100,737 binary SAV-effect annotations (neutral: 39,700, effect: 61,037) from 9594 proteins.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is one released version of the software rather than a family of checkpoints: pyproject.toml gives the package as vespa-effect version 1.0.2 at the commit read here, and the trained models ship inside the repository as three files, ProtT5cons_checkpoint.pt for the conservation predictor and one pickle each for VESPA and VESPAl. A result should name the package version or the commit, and the ProtT5 weights used for the embeddings, because those are downloaded separately at run time into the cache folder the command names. The README also offers an experimental install of the v0.9.0-beta release from GitHub.

sections.title: Precomputed predictions and services
sections.body: Some predictions are published rather than computed. The README points to precomputed VESPA and VESPAl predictions for 39 deep mutational scanning experiments in the paper's supplementary file 3, and to VESPAl predictions for the whole human proteome and for the fly proteome on Zenodo. The paper says the methods are also available through bioembeddings.com, the repository and PredictProtein.

run_guide.summary: Install the pip package and score every possible single amino acid substitution in a FASTA file with VESPA.
prerequisites: Python at least 3.8 and below 3.11, as pyproject.toml requires.
A GPU: the README recommends at least 12 GB of VRAM for the embeddings and says the same applies to running VESPA, and that the log-odds step requires a GPU.
A FASTA file of wild-type sequences, and optionally a mutations file.
Disk space for the ProtT5 weights, which are downloaded into the cache folder on first run.

steps.explanation: The install the README prefers. It brings the trained VESPA model with it.

steps.title: Run VESPA on a FASTA file
steps.explanation: The README quickstart with the vespa flag added, which the README says generates VESPA predictions as well as VESPAl ones and needs a GPU. The cache folder keeps the ProtT5 weights between runs.
steps.source_locator: README: Quickstart and its optional notes

quotes.text: If you have a GPU available you can generate **VESPA** predictions by adding `--vespa` to the code line above.

steps.title: Or run the four substeps
steps.shell:
vespa_emb data/sequences.fasta -o data/embeddings.h5  --prott5_weights_cache data/cache
vespa_conspred data/embeddings.h5 -o data/conspred.h5
vespa_logodds data/sequences.fasta -o data/logodds.h5
vespa_run --vespa data/conspred_probs.h5 data/sequences.fasta --T5_input data/logodds.h5 --output predictions/
steps.explanation: The four README substeps: embed, predict conservation, extract log-odds ratios, then score. Each line is the README's own command. Note that the conservation step writes conspred.h5 while the run step reads conspred_probs.h5, as the README prints them.

outputs: A vespa_run_directory, or the output directory given, holding one semicolon separated CSV per sequence with a row per substitution and its score, plus map.json linking file numbers to sequence IDs.
Optionally an HDF5 file with a 20 by L matrix per sequence, where fields that were not computed hold -1.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository README at commit 34fd1ab1b7fdc2b4e1a241fdae1db5c2f09d8944 and have not been executed by Rewire.
The README's substep file names are inconsistent between the conservation step and the run step; they are reproduced as printed.
The ProtT5 weights are downloaded at run time, so the exact language model revision used is not pinned by the sources.

notes: VESPA and VESPAl come from one repository, one pip package and one paper, so records 13-vespa and 14-vespal share their sources and differ only in which pipeline steps and which model file they describe; they should not be merged, because the README treats them as two models with different inputs and different hardware needs. The trained models are not a separate weights release: they ship inside the repository and the package, so the weights licence is the package licence, AGPL-3.0-or-later, which is copyleft. No release date is stated, so structured.released is null. Two file names in the README's substeps do not line up (conspred.h5 written, conspred_probs.h5 read); the run guide reproduces them as printed and says so.
